open_questions: Phase-curve amplitude_ppm 54.35 ratio_to_depth 0.1107 and excess_noise_sig 8.086 suggest additional variability that needs ground-based photometry and spectroscopy to confirm if blended or stellar spots
Why some sectors show effectively no dip (52: -21 ppm, 53: 19 ppm, 60: 59 ppm) while others show >1400 ppm requires targeted follow-up to test
dossier.public_summary: TESS shows a shallow 490 ppm dip every 14.8 days on a small K dwarf, but the depth measured deep in only a few transits and not at all in others shows the signal is not steady and comes from three strong outliers. A secondary-like dip and measurable phase variation along with no clear on-target centroid make a false alarm or distant eclipsing blend a better explanation than a planet.

reasons.why: Depth changes by factor ~15 between sectors, from ~0 to ~1400 ppm, far larger than expected for a planet; sector_depths_by_source verdict changes_within_a_source with p_constant 1.3638580601183292e-05 in SPOC 2-min and 5.934296816798165e-15 in TESS-SPOC
Individual transit depths are inconsistent; top 3 transits contribute 0.789 of the signal with outliers at 2628, 2302, 1998 ppm versus ~500 ppm average, classic few-event false alarm

Significant secondary dip at phase 0.3918 with snr 6.365 comparable to brightest spot (0.9699), depth 243 ppm ~48% of primary 490.8 ppm, inconsistent with a small planet and favours a stellar/eclipsing binary despite odd_even.diff_sigma 1.834

No centroid localization on-target; neighbours could_cause 21 within 150 arcsec but plausible_within_1px 0, and depth variability together with low xgboost planet_rank 0.14 supports a spurious/correlated-variability origin rather than a planet
